facts.claim: "Last Breath" is a song by Ye (Kanye West) featuring Mexican rapper Peso Pluma, from Ye's twelfth studio album, Bully.

The song was first premiered with other Bully songs at a private post-Grammy Awards event Ye hosted in Los Angeles on February 2, 2025. It was also on Bully V1, the short film that accompanied demo versions of the album.
It was first released as a two-track single on June 27, 2025, alongside "Losing Your Mind". The original single did not include Peso Pluma's vocals.
An Audiomack page lists the track from BULLY with a July 4, 2025 release date and a ℗ 2025 YZY/gamma credit.
The song originated around October 2024 in the early Bully sessions. Ty Dolla $ign wrote the earliest known reference version in English, and DJ Fai helped translate it into Spanish.

Credits list Ye on vocals, writing, production, vocal production and programming. Peso Pluma is credited on vocals and writing, and Ty Dolla $ign on writing and vocal production. Johnscott Stanford played bass guitar and recorded, mixed and mastered the track, as did Josh Schuback and Nkenge 1x.
Wikipedia lists the producers as Kanye West and Sheffmade. Rate Your Music credits Sheffmade as co-producer and Ty Dolla $ign as vocal producer.
Engineer Josh Schuback asked his mentor and fellow engineer John Scott to come to Tokyo to work on Bully. Scott added bass guitar to three of its tracks.

Ye shared an updated version with Peso Pluma on the hook and most of the second verse on March 19, 2026, the day after the Bully film was released. He then posted a new tracklist saying the album would contain "no AI".
The song debuted at No. 5 on Billboard's Hot Latin Songs chart (dated April 11), Ye's first top 10 on that chart. It also debuted at No. 6 on Latin Streaming Songs.

research.lineage: The song is a bilingual Latin-pop and regional Mexican-flavored hip-hop collaboration. One fan wiki compares it to "DRUNK" from Ye and Ty Dolla $ign's VULTURES 2 (2024) and says it departs from Ye's usual sound.

draft:
Halfway through **Last Breath**, after a run of Spanish lines about tears, chaos and being called crazy, the song drops into plain English: "Okay, you win, babe, you're right." It doesn't sound like a concession. It sounds like a white flag waved by someone too tired to argue and too proud to mean it. That gap between what's said and what's felt is the whole song.

The hook is a plea that works two ways. "Bésame, mamá" asks for a kiss the way she knows how, and the next line turns on *déjame*, a word that can mean "let me" or "leave me." The narrator asks for closeness and for release in the same breath, over and over, and never picks one. The verses fill in the fight around that wish: nights spent far away, too much Clase Azul, a denial of whatever she's been saying, then a quick turn to blame her for the mess. Self-justification and real hurt sit right next to each other. When the song finally lands in English, it shows both at once. The last section asks her to come and hold him, then closes the door: "But you'll never control me." He wants to be held, and he can't stand being held onto.

The track came from the early sessions for Ye's album *Bully* around October 2024. Ty Dolla $ign wrote the earliest known version in English, and DJ Fai helped carry it into Spanish. That history makes the English lines feel like the original confession showing through. Ye is credited with vocals, writing, production and programming, with Sheffmade as co-producer and Ty Dolla $ign on vocal production. Johnscott Stanford is credited on bass guitar. The song was first released without Peso Pluma. Ye later shared a version with the Mexican rapper on the hook and most of the second verse, and the song debuted at No. 5 on Billboard's Hot Latin Songs, Ye's first top 10 on that chart. Fans have compared it to "DRUNK" from *VULTURES 2* and called it a departure from Ye's usual sound.

The arrangement keeps things close and calm, which makes the words cut harder. A clean electric guitar sits beside Ye's voice, which carries a light auto-tune sheen and stays smooth and unhurried. A low, steady bass line comes in under them, then a simple drum machine pattern. The mix is dry and polished, with no room sound to hide in. The tempo is moderate and relaxed. Nothing swells or breaks. The steadiness is the point: the music stays composed while the lyrics slide from begging to accusing to giving up.

It's a breakup argument sung like a lullaby, and it sticks because you catch yourself wanting what the narrator wants: to be kissed, to be let go, and to stay untouchable, all at the same time.
